title: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Signatures
subtitle: How a domain signs the email it sends, so receivers can check the mail really passed through it unchanged.
summary: DKIM lets a domain put a cryptographic signature on an email message. The signature goes in a DKIM-Signature header field, and the matching public key is published in the signer's DNS. A receiving server fetches the key, recomputes two hashes and learns that the named domain took responsibility for the message and that the signed parts were not altered on the way. It does not say the message is good, only whose name stands behind it.

plainLanguage.summary: DKIM lets a domain add a cryptographic signature to an email message. The signature goes in a DKIM-Signature header, and the matching public key is published in the signer's DNS. A receiving server fetches the key and checks two hashes. A valid signature shows that the named domain takes responsibility for the message and that the signed parts were not altered. It does not show that the message is good.

questions: what does the dkim-signature header mean
where is the dkim public key stored
what is the difference between relaxed and simple canonicalization

tldr.problem: Email has no built-in way to show which organization really sent a message, or that it was not altered in transit.
tldr.mechanism: The sending domain hashes the body and chosen headers, signs the hash with a private key and adds a DKIM-Signature header. The receiver looks up the public key in DNS at selector._domainkey.domain and checks it.
tldr.outcome: A verified signature gives the receiver a trustworthy domain name to attach reputation to, with no certificate authority involved. It does not stop spoofing of other domains by itself, which is why DMARC builds on it.

today: DKIM is in use on a large share of legitimate email today. Major mailbox providers verify it, and large senders sign with it. Receivers use it alongside SPF and DMARC (RFC 7489) when deciding what to do with a message. Later RFCs changed the cryptography: RFC 8301 removed rsa-sha1 and set stricter key-size rules, and RFC 8463 added the Ed25519-SHA256 signature method. The framing in this RFC (selectors, tags, canonicalization, the DNS record) is unchanged.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) lets a person, role or organization claim responsibility for a message by associating a domain name they are authorized to use with it. The claim is backed by a cryptographic signature, and the verifier gets the matching public key by querying the signer's own domain.

The RFC lists what makes DKIM different from earlier signing schemes such as S/MIME and OpenPGP: the signature lives in a header field, so ordinary mail clients are not confused by it; there is no dependency on well-known certificate authorities; no new protocol or service is needed for key distribution; and a failed verification does not force the message to be rejected. DKIM makes no attempt at encryption, and archiving is not a design goal.

This RFC obsoletes RFC 4871 and RFC 5672, folding the original specification and its errata update into one document. It is also published as STD 76.
sections.plainLanguage: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) lets a person or organization take responsibility for a message by tying a domain name they are authorized to use to it. A cryptographic signature backs this claim. The verifier gets the public key by querying the signer's domain. DKIM does not encrypt anything.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
DKIM was built to fit the email system that already exists. It is meant to be transparent to the fullest extent possible, to need minimal new infrastructure, to be implementable without changes to mail clients, to be deployable incrementally, and to allow signing to be delegated to a third party.

Two ideas stand out. First, DKIM separates the identity of the signer from the apparent author of the message. The signing domain, called the SDID (d=), is what a signature vouches for, and it is not required to match any address in the message. Second, key management is as simple as possible: the verifier asks the signer's domain directly for the public key, normally through DNS, instead of going through a certificate authority.

A signature only says that the hashed content has not changed since it was signed. It says nothing else about protecting the end-to-end integrity of the message, and nothing about whether the content is trustworthy.
sections.plainLanguage: DKIM fits the existing email system. It needs no changes to mail clients and little new infrastructure, and signing can be delegated to a third party. The signing domain (the d= tag) is what the signature vouches for. It need not match any address in the message.

sections.title: The DKIM-Signature Header Field
sections.content:
Everything a verifier needs to start is in one header field, DKIM-Signature, whose value is a list of tag=value pairs separated by semicolons. Unknown tags are ignored by verifiers, but they are still included in the signature calculation.

Seven tags are required: v=1 (version), a= (algorithm), d= (the signing domain), s= (the selector), h= (which header fields were signed), bh= (hash of the canonicalized body) and b= (the signature itself, a base64 value). Optional tags include c= (canonicalization, default simple/simple), i= (the agent or user identifier), l= (a body length limit), q= (query method, dns/txt), t= (timestamp), x= (expiration) and z= (copied header fields for diagnostics).

The From header field must always be listed in h=. The header field should be placed at the top of the header block, like a trace field.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything a verifier needs is in the DKIM-Signature header field, a list of tag=value pairs. Seven tags are required: version, algorithm, signing domain (d=), selector (s=), the signed header fields (h=), the body hash (bh=) and the signature itself (b=).

sections.title: Canonicalization and Hashing
sections.content:
Mail systems often make small changes in transit, such as re-wrapping long lines or changing runs of spaces. Canonicalization prepares the message before hashing so that harmless changes do not break the signature. Two algorithms exist for headers and for the body, and the c= tag names them as header/body. With no c= tag, both default to simple.

simple tolerates almost nothing. For the body it only ignores empty lines at the end. relaxed lowercases header field names, unfolds continuation lines, collapses runs of whitespace to a single space and strips whitespace around the colon and at line ends.

Signing then needs two hashes. First, the canonicalized body (cut to l= octets if that tag is present) is hashed and the result goes into bh=. Second, the header fields listed in h=, in that order, followed by the DKIM-Signature field itself with an empty b=, are hashed and that hash is signed with the private key to produce b=.

Canonicalization only prepares the data for hashing. It never changes the message that is actually sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail systems often make small changes in transit, such as re-wrapping lines. Canonicalization normalizes the message before hashing so such changes do not break the signature. The "simple" setting tolerates almost no change, and "relaxed" ignores differences in whitespace and header case. The signer then hashes the body and the chosen headers.

sections.title: Keys in DNS
sections.content:
Instead of certificates, DKIM publishes public keys in DNS. A key lives in a TXT record at selector._domainkey.domain, where the selector comes from the s= tag and the domain from d=. A selector lets one domain have many keys at once, so a company can use separate keys for different mail streams or rotate keys without a flag day.

The record is itself a tag=value list. v=DKIM1 (if present, it must be first), k= is the key type (default rsa), p= holds the base64 public key, h= and s= restrict hash algorithms and service types, n= carries human notes, and t= carries flags. The flag y means the domain is testing DKIM and verifiers must not treat failing mail differently from unsigned mail. The flag s says the signer's i= domain must match d= exactly instead of allowing subdomains. An empty p= means the key has been revoked.

Signers must use RSA keys of at least 1024 bits for long-lived keys, and verifiers must be able to check keys from 512 to 2048 bits. A later RFC tightened this guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: DKIM publishes public keys in DNS, not in certificates. A key lives in a TXT record at selector._domainkey.domain. The selector lets a domain have several keys at once, for example for different mail streams or for key rotation.

sections.title: Signer and Verifier Actions
sections.content:
A signer decides whether to sign, picks a key and selector, normalizes the message so it will arrive in the form that was signed, chooses the header fields (the RFC suggests From, Reply-To, Subject, Date, To, Cc, and similar), computes the hashes and inserts the new DKIM-Signature header field above any others. A message may carry several signatures, for example from the author's domain and from a mailing-list service. Each is evaluated on its own merits.

A verifier extracts the signature, strictly validates its syntax, fetches the key from DNS, then checks the body hash against bh= and the signature against the header hash. Results are PERMFAIL for permanent problems (bad syntax, no key, revoked key, body hash or signature mismatch) and TEMPFAIL when the DNS lookup cannot be answered. Verification failure should not by itself cause rejection, and a cryptographic failure must never provoke a 4xx SMTP reply. Results are often passed on in an Authentication-Results header field (RFC 5451).
sections.plainLanguage: A signer chooses a key and selector, picks the header fields to sign, computes the hashes and adds a DKIM-Signature header. A message may carry several signatures. A verifier fetches the key from DNS, checks the body hash and the signature, and reports a permanent or temporary failure if something is wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC spends a lot of space on what DKIM does not protect against. A valid signature proves a domain signed the message, not that the message is honest. A spammer can send a message through a well-known signing service and then replay the signed copy to many recipients, borrowing the signer's reputation. The x= expiration tag is explicitly not an anti-replay defense.

Other risks include a stolen private key, which lets an attacker sign as the domain, and the l= body length limit, which leaves everything after the limit unsigned so an attacker can append content. The RFC advises signers to be wary of l= and assessors to consider ignoring signatures that use it. The relaxed body algorithm allows crude ASCII-art tricks by changing spacing. Extra header fields can be added after signing; a signer can list a name in h= one more time than it appears to make an added copy break the signature.

DKIM itself attaches no policy to a missing or failing signature. A receiver should not reject mail solely because it has no signature or an unverifiable one, which is what later work such as DMARC addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: A valid signature proves that a domain signed the message, not that the message is honest. A spammer can replay a signed copy to many recipients. A stolen private key lets an attacker sign as the domain, and the l= body length tag leaves everything after the limit unsigned.

viz.caption: What DKIM sets out to be

items.title: Fits existing email
items.text: The signature is a header field, so unaware mail systems and clients simply pass it along.

items.title: No certificate authority
items.text: The verifier asks the signing domain for its public key, normally through DNS.

items.title: Signer is not the author
items.text: The signed domain (d=) is separate from the From address, and it can belong to a third party.

items.title: Failure is not rejection
items.text: A signature that fails to verify is treated like no signature, not as proof of fraud.

items.title: Replay
items.text: A genuine signed message can be re-sent to many people, borrowing the signer's reputation.

items.title: Stolen keys
items.text: A compromised private key lets an attacker sign as the domain until the key record is removed.

items.title: Body length limit (l=)
items.text: Anything beyond the limit is unsigned and can be appended by an intermediary.

items.title: Extra header fields
items.text: List a header name in h= one extra time to make an added copy invalidate the signature.
